What Keynes found when he opened Newton’s trunks
A flawed, com­plex man, and the ac­ci­dents that raised him

brief.head: All fit, no theory
brief.text: Kepler’s laws fit Tycho Brahe’s data beau­ti­fully, Ajay Shah said, but like an AI model they could not say why. Newton de­rived them from first prin­ci­ples. {007-C01}

brief.head: Ivory tower, no thanks
brief.text: Researchers who only look at each other are fun­da­men­tally ster­ile, Ajay Shah said. Ideas and mar­kets are one con­tin­uum: firms bring hard prob­lems, thinkers fuel busi­ness. {007-C04}

brief.head: Defeats that mobilised
brief.text: Almost every satya­graha Gandhi led failed in its im­me­di­ate aims, Amit Varma said. Yet each mo­bilised or­di­nary peo­ple, which no leader be­fore him had man­aged. {007-C06}

brief.head: More dots, please
brief.text: Gandhi, Ram Guha writes, said he did not need to read be­cause he could see the world un­fold. Amit Varma called it a ra­tio­nal­i­sa­tion: read­ing gives more dots to con­nect. {007-C13}

brief.head: Wrong, and wonderful
brief.text: Ajay Shah dis­agrees with John Maynard Keynes on al­most all his eco­nom­ics, and counts him among the most won­der­ful peo­ple who ever lived. Amit Varma said ditto. {007-C12}

thought.label: Thought for the day
thought.text: We should not be rev­er­en­tial, we should be an­a­lyt­i­cal, we should un­der­stand.
thought.who: Ajay Shah, urging an analytical rather than devotional reading of Gandhi and his ideas

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on Newton, Gandhi and history
lead.head: The alchemist and the accident

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 7

body: Is ge­nius made by its times, or does it ar­rive by ac­ci­dent? Ajay Shah an­swered with Isaac Newton, Amit Varma with Mohandas Gandhi, and they did not quite agree.

Shah told Newton’s story in three chap­ters. The first is the one chil­dren hear: plague shut down Cambridge, Newton went to live with his grand­mother, and in one fever­ish year he built ev­ery­thing. {007-S02}

The sec­ond came from John Maynard Keynes, who bought many of Newton’s pa­pers and found them full of alchemy and the Bible. “He says Newton was not the first man of the age of rea­son, he was the last of the ma­gi­cians,” Shah said. {007-C02}
The third came from Boris Hessen, a Soviet physi­cist and philoso­pher who asked, in 1931, what kind of so­ci­ety pro­duces a Newton.
## England’s con­di­tions

Hessen’s an­swer, as Shah re­layed it, was 17th-century England: Protestant enough for free thought, a sea­far­ing power learn­ing op­tics and nav­i­ga­tion, and pro­tected by the Magna Carta tra­di­tion.
“So Newton doesn’t come out of thin air,” Shah said. Gene ex­pres­sion was his metaphor: a so­ci­ety that pro­tects its mav­er­icks lets its Newtons flour­ish. {007-C03}

Varma ac­cepted the point, up to a point. Newton could not have been Newton in Spain, he said, but the times did not make him in­evitable. That such a per­son was there at that time was “a mar­vel­lous ac­ci­dent of his­tory”.
## Gandhi, the out­lier

Gandhi, Varma ar­gued, was the coun­terex­am­ple: a black swan. His in­flu­ences, Tolstoy, Ruskin and a dog­matic veg­e­tar­ian so­ci­ety in London, were hap­haz­ard next to those of the Congress mod­er­ates, who read Mill, Bentham and Adam Smith.

His rise was an ac­ci­dent too. Gandhi al­lied with the Khilafat move­ment to re­store the caliphate in Turkey, while ask­ing for India’s in­de­pen­dence. Varma called it ut­terly in­co­her­ent, yet it made Gandhi the leader of the Congress in 1920.

Shah dis­agreed. Gandhi drew on the best of Hindu and Jain phi­los­o­phy, he said, and faced the great ques­tion of his age: how to rec­on­cile India with the West. “You should think that there were a large num­ber of lot­ter­ies and one per­son got ex­pressed,” he said. {007-C05}

Nonviolence also suited the op­po­nent, Shah ar­gued: under French, Belgian or Japanese rule, a free­dom fighter would soon have been jailed and killed. “It re­quired British de­cency for these kinds of ideas to sur­vive and flour­ish.”
## Freedom was com­ing any­way
On one thing the hosts agreed: the story we grow up on, in which the Congress fought the British and India won its free­dom, is too sim­ple.

Varma pointed to a Britain broke after the Second World War. Shah added the end of the first glob­al­i­sa­tion in 1913, Europe’s wars, and the Atlantic Charter, which tied American help to a post-colonial fu­ture.
“My coun­ter­fac­tual in his­tory is there is no sce­nario under which British rule would have lasted in a sig­nif­i­cant way be­yond 1950, 1955,” Shah said. {007-C09}

Hindsight, Varma warned, makes the un­cer­tain look in­evitable. “Before it hap­pened, it was prob­a­bilis­tic. Everything is prob­a­bilis­tic, it’s up in the air. After it’s hap­pened, it’s 100% hap­pened.”

The dis­cus­sion closed on luck. Varma read from his col­umn *Luck is All Around* on the odds against any­one ex­ist­ing; Shah told lis­ten­ers they were unique strings in DNA’s four-letter al­pha­bet, and should wake up and do amaz­ing things.
Newton, Shah noted, had been shipped off in a lock­down. “What do you have to show for your lock­down achieve­ments?”

second.label: The road to Partition
second.head: The gentleman walks out
second.deck: Amit Varma on how Gandhi’s rise broke the last great moderate
body: With Gokhale and Pherozeshah Mehta gone, Mohammed Ali Jinnah was the last great mod­er­ate in the Congress, Amit Varma said: deeply ed­u­cated, ra­tio­nal, and ex­pected to lead the party. Ram Guha tells how Jinnah once con­sid­ered going to South Africa, where he and Gandhi might have be­come busi­ness part­ners. {#partners}

Gandhi’s takeover in 1920 broke him. Jinnah said he was part­ing com­pany with the Congress and Gandhi, be­cause he did not be­lieve in work­ing up mass hys­te­ria. His sense of self badly hurt, he moved to­wards the two-nation the­ory. {007-S11}
Varma traced Partition, and fis­sures India still wres­tles with, back to that mo­ment. A ra­tio­nal man of deep learn­ing, he said, be­came a com­pletely dif­fer­ent per­son.

quote.text: I do not be­lieve in work­ing up mass hys­te­ria. Politics is a gentleman’s game.

third.head: The outlaw at the Mint

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the alchemist at the Mint

body: Isaac Newton spent his life on alchemy, and it was against the law. In 1404, Ajay Shah said, the British gov­ern­ment had banned all forms of alchemy to pro­tect its mo­nop­oly on coinage. {#alchemyban}

Nobody then knew that base met­als can­not be turned into gold, and the state could not take the risk. Debase the cur­rency, Shah said, and the whole mon­e­tary sys­tem breaks down. He was, he ad­mit­ted, steal­ing words from ner­vous pol­i­cy­mak­ers of today.

“Newton was this law­breaker and in case that irony is not ad­e­quate, late in his life, Newton be­came the mas­ter of the mint,” Shah said: the gov­er­nor of the cen­tral bank, in today’s terms. {007-S04}
Amit Varma’s ver­dict: putting an al­chemist in charge of the mint “would be like a poacher be­com­ing a game­keeper”. {007-J06}

box.title: The essay that unmasked Newton
box.text: *Newton, the Man*, John Maynard Keynes’s paper, is the source of the “last of the ma­gi­cians” view. Ajay Shah, who dis­agrees with nearly all of Keynes’s eco­nom­ics, rec­om­mends his *Essays in Persuasion* and *Essays in Biography*: “Everybody should dream of writ­ing like that.” {007-R05}

sections.label: Newton, part one
sections.head: First the data, then the why
sections.caption: Newton’s lone-genius legend
body: Ajay Shah’s first win­dow on Isaac Newton is the one chil­dren learn. Plague shut Cambridge, Newton went to a vil­lage to live with his grand­mother, and in one fever­ish year he “just cre­ated an im­mense ex­plo­sion in the world of knowl­edge”.

Shah set out the se­quence. The old Greek records of the plan­ets were poor and the mod­els mud­dled: the sun cir­cled the earth, and or­bits had to be pure cir­cles, patched with epicy­cles, “wheels within wheels”. {007-J08}

Copernicus put the sun at the cen­tre but still thought in cir­cles, so his model was only a lit­tle bet­ter. Then Tycho Brahe built the world’s best data set, and Johannes Kepler found three sim­ple laws that fit it with­out ex­plain­ing why. {007-C01}
## First prin­ci­ples

Newton sup­plied the why. His laws of mo­tion, his law of grav­ity and his cal­cu­lus made a first-principles tool­kit from which Kepler’s laws dropped out as a con­se­quence. “What a tri­umph,” Shah said.
Alexander Pope caught the myth in an epi­taph: “Nature and her mys­ter­ies lay hid­den in the night. God said, Let Newton be and all was light.” {007-J09}
How did it hap­pen? Shah could point only to con­cen­tra­tion, which Newton shared with Einstein. Beyond that, he said, “we have no great in­sight”.
~ The party line, he said, is that a ge­nius just hap­pened and should get all the credit. Shah’s sec­ond and third chap­ters made the story “way more in­ter­est­ing”.

quote.text: But sta­tis­ti­cal mod­els, okay? They’re like an AI that it kind of fits the data, but you don’t know any­thing about why it works.

sections.label: Newton, part two
sections.head: Reason in public, gold at home
sections.caption: Keynes and the last of the magicians
body: Many years after Newton, Ajay Shah said, some­one auc­tioned off his pa­pers, in­her­ited from a great-grandfather. John Maynard Keynes turned up and put down 9,000 pounds of his own money for a good chunk of them. {#auction}
The rest, Keynes sniffed, had “doubt­less ended up in America”, which Shah ren­dered as America being “the back­wa­ters where things go to die”. {007-J05}

Keynes was the first to study them, and he was aghast. Newton had spent his life on alchemy and the Bible, count­ing let­ters in scrip­ture for the se­cret of mak­ing gold. He wrote a mil­lion words on alchemy.
## Two Newtons
Keynes’s ver­dict was that Newton was the last of the ma­gi­cians, the place where magic and su­per­sti­tion give way to rea­son. {007-C02}

In pub­lic Newton was clean and ra­tio­nal. Asked how grav­ity worked, he said “I do not make hy­pothe­ses”, which Shah trans­lated as “I do not spec­u­late”. {007-J10} Inside, Shah said, he was a tor­mented man.

The paper, *Newton, the Man*, was meant for 1942, the 300th an­niver­sary of Newton’s birth. The war pushed the con­fer­ence to 1946, in Warsaw, Shah said; Keynes had died, and his brother Geoffrey pre­sented it.
~ Shah saw a les­son for ev­ery­one. Old and new ideas fight in­side all of us, he said, as in Nehru’s line about being a bat­tle­field of ideas.

quote.text: He opened those trunks of ma­te­rial and was just aghast at what was going on. Newton was filled with alchemy and the Bible.

art.caption: Ajay Shah on Keynes and the last of the magicians

sections.label: Newton, part three
sections.head: The making of a Newton
sections.caption: Boris Hessen’s Marxist Newton
body: In 1931 Boris Hessen, a Soviet physi­cist and philoso­pher, ap­plied the Marxist ap­proach to his­tory to Newton. {007-R07} That was still a time, Ajay Shah noted, when Marxists held real in­tel­lec­tual lead­er­ship.

Hessen asked what so­cial and eco­nomic con­di­tions pro­duce a Newton. Shah’s sum­mary of the an­swer began with free­dom. In Italy Giordano Bruno was burnt at the stake and Galileo threat­ened with tor­ture; Protestant England was freer. “A pretty basic thing is you should not be burn­ing mav­er­icks,” Shah said. {#mavericks}

England had also been the great­est sea­far­ing na­tion since it de­stroyed the Spanish Armada in 1588, which meant op­tics, tele­scopes, nav­i­ga­tion and ma­chines. And under the Magna Carta, Newton could break the alchemy law at home with­out fear of a dun­geon. {007-C03}
## Money and ideas

Hessen’s bold­est point, Shah said, was re­ject­ing the “Brahminical” view that ideas stand apart from the base project of mak­ing money. Thinkers fuel busi­ness, and busi­ness brings thinkers its prob­lems. {007-C04}
Amit Varma added that thinkers can be builders: Jeff Bezos, Steve Jobs, Elon Musk and Paul Graham, whose es­says he called “just a trea­sure given to mankind”.
~ Hessen him­self was an out­spo­ken free thinker. In 1936, Shah said, he was mur­dered in one of Stalin’s purges. {007-S05}

quote.text: The well­springs of the in­tel­lec­tual process emerge from de­mands made of the think­ing peo­ple.

art.caption: Ajay Shah on Boris Hessen’s Marxist Newton

sections.label: Gandhi, the case
sections.head: A swan nobody saw coming
sections.caption: Gandhi as a black swan
body: Amit Varma of­fered Mohandas Gandhi as the coun­terex­am­ple to Ajay Shah’s Newton: not a prod­uct of his­tor­i­cal cur­rents but a black swan.

VS Naipaul, Varma noted, called Gandhi the least Indian of the Indian lead­ers. {007-J15} His in­flu­ences were hap­haz­ard: Tolstoy, Ruskin and a London veg­e­tar­ian so­ci­ety as dog­matic as some ve­g­ans today. The Congress mod­er­ates, by con­trast, read Mill, Bentham and Adam Smith.
## Railways, lawyers, doc­tors

Varma read from *Hind Swaraj*, writ­ten in Gandhi’s early for­ties, which rails against rail­ways, lawyers and doc­tors: “Hospitals are in­sti­tu­tions for prop­a­gat­ing sin.” Gandhi him­self later ac­cepted treat­ment from European doc­tors.
When Varma asked Ramachandra Guha how a man so wrong could be right about non­vi­o­lent re­sis­tance, Guha said he was right about the one thing he had per­sonal ex­pe­ri­ence of. {007-S08}
Gandhi’s rise, too, was an ac­ci­dent, Varma ar­gued. His al­liance with the Khilafat move­ment made no sense, yet in 1920 it car­ried him from the mar­gins to the head of the Congress. {007-S10}

~ Varma thinks of him as “Mohandas Gandhi, not Mahatma Gandhi”, a com­plex, tor­tured man. Gandhi’s hun­dred vol­umes of writ­ing are free on­line, and he would have been a blog­ger today, Varma said. {#blogger}

quote.text: But it turns out, and I be­lieve it turns out by ac­ci­dent, to be a strate­gic mas­ter stroke.

sections.label: Gandhi, the reply
sections.head: One ticket in many lotteries
sections.caption: Gandhi and the ripe conditions
body: Ajay Shah would not let Gandhi be a black swan. His moral phi­los­o­phy, Shah said, came from the high phi­los­o­phy of Hinduism and Jainism, on which Tagore and the New Testament were sprin­kled.

Gandhi also faced the great ques­tion of his age, how to fit India and the West to­gether, as any child today grows up with the reg­u­la­tion of AI. The con­di­tions were ripe, Shah said, for some­one to be ex­pressed. {007-C05}

Nonviolence fit­ted the op­po­nent, too. Britain was ruled by lib­eral democ­racy and the rule of law, so an ap­peal to its de­cency worked bet­ter than Subhas Chandra Bose’s call to pick up guns. {007-C10}
## Tactician or sys­tem-builder?

Shah di­vided men of ac­tion into tac­ti­cians, who tack with the wind, and sys­tem-builders, who seek co­her­ence and so can admit being wrong. Gandhi, he said, was a do-it-yourself philoso­pher. {007-C08}

Varma dis­agreed. Gandhi was a tac­ti­cian, he ar­gued, with a small set of tac­tics ap­plied rigidly; *Hind Swaraj* is too in­co­her­ent to be phi­los­o­phy. Still, he said, both would agree that ev­ery­one should read Gandhi’s writ­ings and study his life.

~ Shah also cred­ited Europe’s self-destruction with eas­ing India’s path. “If Wagner and Russian forces are going to fight it out with each other, it’s eas­ier for Ukraine to go free,” he said. {007-J20}

quote.text: If you are only a tac­ti­cal man of ac­tion, noth­ing is wrong. Everything is ex­pe­di­ent.

art.caption: Amit Varma on Gandhi and the ripe conditions

quote.text: It tells you how char­ac­ter is con­tin­gent, how ev­ery­thing you claim to be­lieve in may be con­tin­gent, how we are driven by in­cen­tives we can­not un­der­stand.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: A gift of data, a donkey’s god, a mentor’s order and a wartime bargain

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the data behind Newton’s triumph
stories.head: A gift for the man he detested
body: Long be­fore Isaac Newton, as­tron­omy ran on old Greek records of the plan­ets and stars, and the data were poor. The mod­els were worse, Ajay Shah said: the sun went round the earth, and every orbit had to be a pure cir­cle.
When the cir­cles did not fit the data, as­tronomers added epicy­cles, wheels within wheels. It was com­pli­cated, Shah said, and it was a mess.

Copernicus had the sim­ple idea that the earth goes round the sun. But he still thought in cir­cles, so his model fit only a lit­tle bet­ter. People mock those who op­posed him, Shah said, but as sci­ence the gains were not great.

The break­through came from a Danish lord, Tycho Brahe, liv­ing off the coast on the is­land of Uraniborg. “You can’t make these things up,” Shah said. Tycho gave his whole life to mak­ing the world’s best data set on the move­ments of the plan­ets and stars.
As his life came to an end, he knew that only one man could make sense of it: Johannes Kepler, whom he truly de­tested. Without Kepler, his life’s work would be point­less. {007-S01}
“So at the end of his life he swal­lowed his pride and he handed this data on a plat­ter to Kepler,” Shah said.
~ Kepler found three beau­ti­ful, sim­ple laws. The plan­ets move in el­lipses. They sweep out equal areas in equal times. And the square of the time is pro­por­tional to the cube of the ra­dius.
stories.why: Breakthroughs rest on pa­tient, unglam­orous data work, and here on a man who put his life’s work above his pride. Kepler’s laws fit the data with­out say­ing why; it took Newton’s first prin­ci­ples to ex­plain them. {007-C01}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Tycho Brahe’s gift to Kepler

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on his old college’s irreverent past
stories.head: The professor’s donkey god
body: In the 1890s the re­former Gopal Ganesh Agarkar, a mod­er­ate leader who died too young, was teach­ing a bi­ol­ogy class at Fergusson College in Pune.
At one point he asked: “If don­keys had a god, what would that god look like?” After a few mo­ments of si­lence, Amit Varma said, Agarkar an­swered with a ges­ture. {007-S07}
This was in the late 1800s, be­fore the 20th cen­tury had even begun, and the col­lege was called, Varma said, “the hot­bed of athe­ism”.
~ Varma stud­ied at Fergusson a cen­tury later. “It al­most breaks my heart that when I was in Fergusson College, I did not know any of this,” he said. He doubts it could be that place today.
stories.why: Intellectual dar­ing is not a ratchet that only turns one way. A col­lege in late-19th-century Pune al­lowed an ir­rev­er­ence in its class­rooms that, Amit Varma sus­pects, might be im­pos­si­ble there now.
stories.postscript: Fergusson was also where Gandhi first met his hero, Gopal Krishna Gokhale, on a walk around the grounds.

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a mentor’s last request to Gandhi
stories.head: Look before you lead
body: Gandhi first met his hero, Gopal Krishna Gokhale, in the early 1890s on a walk around the grounds of Fergusson College. When he came back from South Africa for good, the mod­er­ates were dying out and Gokhale was ill.
Gokhale had read *Hind Swaraj* and was alarmed, Amit Varma said, be­cause the ideas were non­sense. He saw in Gandhi a man of great con­vic­tion and en­ergy who did not yet know the coun­try.
So he asked for a prom­ise. “For the next one year you will not take part in any po­lit­i­cal ac­tiv­ity. You will go around the coun­try and you will just see things.” {007-S09}
~ A month later Gokhale died. Gandhi kept the prom­ise, and as a trib­ute to Gokhale, for rea­sons Varma does not know, he did it bare­foot. {#barefoot}

quote.text: He was a lit­tle wacko in some ways.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Gokhale’s last instruction

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on America’s hand in Indian independence
stories.head: Roosevelt’s price for a rescue
body: When the Second World War began in 1939, Ajay Shah said, Roosevelt was clear that America had to be in it on Britain’s side. But a pow­er­ful iso­la­tion­ism held him back.

It had three strands. Some racist na­tion­al­ists would hap­pily have done busi­ness with Hitler. Many Americans were ex­hausted by the First World War and the flu that fol­lowed it. And a mis­trust of em­pire dated back to the American re­volt of 1776.

Helping Britain could look like sup­port­ing the British Empire, which Churchill was de­ter­mined to pro­tect. Between September 1939 and December 1941 the two lead­ers ar­gued it out, and the re­sult was the Atlantic Charter.
“Roosevelt ba­si­cally said to the British that we will come to your aid. But we have to plan for a post-colonial fu­ture,” Shah said. {007-S12}
~ Lend-Lease came with con­di­tions about India, Shah said.
stories.why: Indian in­de­pen­dence, in Ajay Shah’s telling, was shaped in Washington and London as well as by the free­dom move­ment. The his­tory is well es­tab­lished, he said, but not taught ad­e­quately in India, and these are sto­ries worth telling.

quiz.q: Who handed the world’s best planetary data to Johannes Kepler, a man he detested?
quiz.a: Tycho Brahe, the Danish lord, who swal­lowed his pride at the end of his life.

quiz.q: After reading Newton’s papers, what did Keynes call him instead of the first man of reason?
quiz.a: The last of the ma­gi­cians, a man torn be­tween alchemy and rea­son.

quiz.q: Why, according to Ajay Shah, was Newton’s alchemy research against the law?
quiz.a: In 1404 the British gov­ern­ment had banned alchemy, fear­ing de­base­ment of the cur­rency.

quiz.q: What question did Gopal Ganesh Agarkar put to his biology class at Fergusson College?
quiz.a: If don­keys had a god, what would that god look like?

quiz.q: What promise did the ailing Gokhale extract from Gandhi on his return to India?
quiz.a: A year out of pol­i­tics, trav­el­ling the coun­try to ob­serve; Gandhi did it bare­foot.

quiz.q: Asked by a journalist about Western civilisation, what did Gandhi reply, as Shah told it?
quiz.a: That it would be a good idea, a sign of Britain’s lost re­spect.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 7. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Mahatma Gandhi (Elliott & Fry, public domain); Isaac Newton (Godfrey Kneller, public domain); Mohammad Ali Jinnah (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); John Maynard Keynes (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Philip Pullman (graphed by Adrian Hon, http://mssv.net/, CC BY-SA 2.0). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon, Apple and Open Library.

shelf.title: The White Crow Books and Coffee
shelf.why: Ajay calls it Bombay’s great new tourist at­trac­tion.

shelf.title: The bookshop ritual: buying each other books
shelf.why: An easy rit­ual to start with friends that in­tro­duces each of you to books you would never have picked your­self.

shelf.title: The Ascent of Man
shelf.creator: Jacob Bronowski
shelf.why: Bronowski’s his­tory of sci­en­tific thought, the writ­ten com­pan­ion to the TV se­ries that shaped Ajay from child­hood and fed his sto­ries of sci­en­tific out­laws.

shelf.title: Newton, the Man
shelf.creator: John Maynard Keynes
shelf.why: It is the source of the ‘last of the magicians’ view of Newton, show­ing the al­chemist and Bible scholar be­hind the ra­tio­nal front.

shelf.title: Essays in Persuasion
shelf.creator: John Maynard Keynes
shelf.why: Ajay dis­agrees with nearly all of Keynes’s eco­nom­ics, but sees him as a mas­ter writer who knew the world.

shelf.title: Essays in Biography
shelf.creator: John Maynard Keynes
shelf.why: Read it as a model of beau­ti­ful writ­ing and sharp in­sight into peo­ple, from an econ­o­mist Ajay ar­gues with but deeply ad­mires.

shelf.title: The social and economic roots of Newton’s Principia
shelf.creator: Boris Hessen
shelf.why: It chal­lenged the great man the­ory by trac­ing Newton to English con­di­tions: free­dom, sea power, tin­ker­ing.

shelf.title: Epitaph on Sir Isaac Newton
shelf.creator: Alexander Pope
shelf.why: It sums up in one cou­plet the myth of the sud­den lone ge­nius, which the rest of the chap­ter com­pli­cates.

shelf.title: The Discovery of India
shelf.creator: Jawaharlal Nehru
shelf.why: The book Ajay calls ‘lit­er­ally the book that in­vents the idea of India’: an idea grounded in his­tory and free of ha­tred, in a mod­ern syn­the­sis com­fort­able with sci­ence and lib­eral democ­racy.

shelf.title: The Power Broker
shelf.creator: Robert Caro
shelf.why: Caro’s mas­ter­piece works on three lev­els: a bi­og­ra­phy of Robert Moses, a bi­og­ra­phy of New York re­shaped by top-down plan­ning, and a study of how power cor­rupts an ide­al­is­tic man.

shelf.title: The Essays of Paul Graham
shelf.creator: Paul Graham
shelf.why: Free es­says that Amit calls ‘a trea­sure given to mankind’: mod­els of sim­ple, clear writ­ing, each work­shopped for months, by some­one who also builds things.

shelf.title: Marginal Revolution, Marginal Revolution University and Emergent Ventures
shelf.creator: Tyler Cowen and Alex Tabarrok
shelf.why: The blog Amit thinks has been the best in the world for 15 years: two econ­o­mists think­ing aloud in clear prose every day, a model for aca­demics and bet­ter sense-making than a newspaper’s eco­nom­ics pages.

shelf.title: Keynes vs. Hayek rap battles: ‘Fear the Boom and Bust’ and ‘Fight of the Century’
shelf.creator: Russ Roberts (lyrics)
shelf.why: A rap bat­tle be­tween ac­tors play­ing Keynes and Hayek, with lyrics by EconTalk’s Russ Roberts, which the hosts rec­om­mend to­gether with its se­quel, Fight of the Century: a de­light­ful way into the clash be­tween the two dom­i­nant eco­nomic schools of the 20th cen­tury.

shelf.title: Conversation and Society (Episode 182 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Russ Roberts
shelf.why: Russ Roberts on the art of con­ver­sa­tion and Adam Smith’s moral phi­los­o­phy, an episode Amit re­mem­bers for its ‘mag­i­cal chemistry’.

shelf.title: His Dark Materials trilogy
shelf.creator: Philip Pullman
shelf.why: Books Amit calls mas­ter­pieces, ask­ing you to trust him blindly; years later they still make him smile or tear up.

shelf.title: The Collected Works of Mahatma Gandhi
shelf.creator: Mohandas Gandhi
shelf.why: Ninety-nine vol­umes, free to read, in which you can watch a man en­gage with the world in writ­ing every day, with un­var­nished hon­esty, like a blog­ger of his time.

shelf.title: Hind Swaraj
shelf.creator: Mohandas Gandhi
shelf.why: Part of our his­tory, and the best ev­i­dence for Amit’s ar­gu­ment that Gandhi was in­co­her­ent on most things but right about non­vi­o­lent re­sis­tance.

shelf.title: The Mahatma and the Poet
shelf.creator: Sabyasachi Bhattacharya (editor)
shelf.why: The Gandhi-Tagore de­bate laid out in full, two great minds dis­agree­ing well: Tagore more rea­soned and right about the dan­gers of na­tion­al­ism, yet see­ing some­thing spe­cial in Gandhi’s force of will.

shelf.title: Gandhi Before India
shelf.creator: Ramachandra Guha
shelf.why: Amit finds the South Africa years, when Gandhi was still form­ing, es­pe­cially in­ter­est­ing, and calls Guha a phe­nom­e­nal his­to­rian.

shelf.title: Gandhi: The Years That Changed the World
shelf.creator: Ramachandra Guha
shelf.why: With the first vol­ume, it gives the full arc.

shelf.title: Great Soul
shelf.creator: Joseph Lelyveld
shelf.why: Lelyveld, a fine writer who has writ­ten widely for the New Yorker, hinted at a ho­mo­sex­ual re­la­tion­ship, partly be­cause the two called each other ‘upper house’ and ‘lower house.’ That was shock­ing enough to get the book banned.

shelf.title: The Good Boatman
shelf.creator: Rajmohan Gandhi
shelf.why: Thematic es­says on Gandhi’s life, from women to caste, that syn­the­sise a vast amount of ma­te­rial: ‘a pow­er­ful book of ideas’ for en­gag­ing with his con­tra­dic­tions, and Amit’s model of a syn­op­tic book.

shelf.title: Understanding Gandhi, Parts 1 and 2 (Episodes 104 and 105 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Ramachandra Guha
shelf.why: Amit’s first two episodes with Ramachandra Guha, on Gandhi, for which Amit read some thirty books, so they dis­til a whole shelf of bi­ogra­phies.

shelf.title: Luck is All Around
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: A short, vivid case for how much luck lies be­hind your ex­is­tence and ev­ery­thing else, and the life les­son that fol­lows: don’t let good luck make you ar­ro­gant or bad luck make you de­featist.

shelf.title: An Area of Darkness
shelf.creator: VS Naipaul
shelf.why: Supports Amit’s ar­gu­ment that Gandhi’s in­flu­ences were un­usual for an Indian leader of his time.

shelf.title: Marching For Salt
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s sur­pris­ing point that in­de­pen­dent India taxed salt far more than the British did, ev­i­dence that the free­dom strug­gle is in­com­plete, and more of his take on Gandhi.

shelf.title: As Tears Go By
shelf.creator: The Rolling Stones
shelf.why: A play­ful mu­si­cal aside at the start of the episode.

laughs.text: Amit opens by telling Ajay he looks like he ‘es­caped from a prison but for­got to take your pa­ja­mas.’ Ajay’s de­fence: it’s get­ting cold, so he bumped up to a full sleeve.

Ajay: ‘I’m a card-carrying econ­o­mist, so in every episode you’re gonna suf­fer some eco­nom­ics.’ Amit re­ports the pro­ducer ask­ing where the card is. Ajay: ‘This is my card, that I will al­ways play an eco­nom­ics card every time I speak with you.’
Ajay slips and says ‘Newton showed up at the auc­tion.’ Amit cor­rects him to Keynes, and Ajay replies: ‘Would be nice if Newton showed up.’

The pa­pers were auc­tioned by some ‘nalayak bachcha’ (good-for-nothing kid). Keynes com­plained the rest had ‘doubt­less ended up in America’, which Ajay ren­ders as ‘America is like the back­wa­ters where things go to die.’
Amit on an al­chemist who had bro­ken the law be­com­ing Master of the Mint: ‘like a poacher be­com­ing a game­keeper.’

Amit re­counts their din­ner ar­gu­ment about free will: Amit said there can’t be any, Ajay said of course there is, and Amit con­cluded ‘we are hav­ing this ar­gu­ment be­cause we can’t help but have it.’

Gandhi and Kallenbach called each other ‘upper house’ and ‘lower house’, pos­si­bly be­cause one de­cided spend­ing and the other had a veto. Cue the quip ‘Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha’, fol­lowed by the re­minder that nei­ther ex­isted then.
Amit on Keynes’s most fa­mous line: ‘In the long run, we are all dead. So, which of course is un­doubt­edly true as well.’
Ajay to the au­di­ence: ‘When there was a great pan­demic, Newton was shipped off in the lock­down, and look what he did with his life. What do you have to show for your lock­down achieve­ments?’

Ajay’s ‘it’s be­com­ing evening’ sets off The Rolling Stones’ ‘As Tears Go By’: ‘It is the evening of the day. What’s the next line?’ ‘I want to hear the chil­dren play.’ ‘Brilliant. I’m so proud of you.’
Newton’s mil­lion words on alchemy: ‘That’s like the Robert Caro book with­out the 200,000 words on Jane Jacobs taken out’ — a nod to The Power Broker.
Epicycles, the ‘wheels within wheels’ that kept or­bits cir­cu­lar: Ajay notes this is where the phrase comes from.
Alexander Pope’s epi­taph, as quoted: ‘Nature and her mys­ter­ies lay hid­den in the night. God said, Let Newton be and all was light.’
Asked how grav­ity ac­tu­ally works, Newton replied ‘I do not make hypotheses’ — which Ajay trans­lates into mod­ern English as ‘I do not spec­u­late.’
VS Naipaul’s re­mark that Gandhi was ‘the least Indian of the Indian lead­ers.’
Gandhi, asked by a jour­nal­ist what he thought of Western civil­i­sa­tion: ‘It would be a good idea.’
Einstein on Gandhi: ‘Generations to come will scarcely be­lieve that such a man would walk this earth in flesh and blood.’ Ajay uses it to focus on the man rather than the out­come.
